caption: Overwrite: a CBTC covered-call vault on Canton
narrate: Overwrite is a covered call vault for C B T C on Canton. Deposit Bitcoin, the vault writes a call against it, and the premium is paid to holders on chain. With a book nobody else can read.

block.sub: A CBTC covered-call vault on Canton

caption: Why this does not exist yet
narrate: Two things are missing today. C B T C holders have no self serve on chain yield on Canton. And on a public chain vault the whole book is readable: depositors, size, strikes, roll timing. Market makers price against that flow, and an institution will not display its Bitcoin position for anyone to read.

block.title: The gap
rows: No self-serve on-chain BTC yield on Canton
On a public chain, the whole book is readable
Institutions will not display their BTC position

caption: One epoch is one full option lifecycle
narrate: So privacy is the product, not a feature. A production epoch is one week. This demo compresses it to seconds, so you can watch a whole one. Every step is a state change on the ledger: deposits open, collateral locks, the vault writes the call, and at expiry exactly one of two settlement paths runs.

caption: The operator's control room: the scheduler is its own process
narrate: This is the operator's control room. The scheduler runs as its own process and drives every transition on a tick. Pausing stops it between ticks, never mid transaction, so stepping is safe. Step, and it settles the expiring call. Step again, and it records the epoch. Resume, and the engine locks collateral for the next epoch, writes a new call, and the market maker pays the premium.

caption: A deposit is a real write to a real ledger
narrate: A depositor can write to it too. Alice deposits half a C B T C. Review is the deliberate confirm before the write, and the app submits to the ledger. Her position comes back as a contract signed by the operator and by Alice, and by nobody else.

caption: Privacy is the Daml signatory model, not a UI filter
narrate: Here is the part that matters. The operator is a signatory on every position, so the operator sees the whole book, and each row reports what that depositor's own session actually returns. Now switch to Alice. The app re-reads the ledger with Alice's own key, server side. She sees her own deposit and her own premium. Bob and Carol are not hidden from her. They are simply not in her view of the ledger.

caption: Settled epochs: aggregate only, no per-holder payout list
narrate: Every settled epoch is recorded as an aggregate report: the settlement price, the strike, the premium, and a depositor count. There is no per holder payout list anywhere in it. Each receipt is visible only to the depositor who received it. The price feed and the market maker here are simulated, and every premium figure is a demo parameter, not market pricing.

caption: The collateral lock runs against the real CIP-56 registry on devnet
narrate: The collateral lock is not a mock. On the Canton hack net the package is uploaded and vetted, and real C B T C is deposited and locked through the vault using the registry's own allocation factory, which is the token standard's lock and settlement primitive. That allocation is still live on the ledger today. The rest of the lifecycle runs on a local Canton sandbox.

caption: At expiry, exactly one of two paths runs
narrate: At expiry, out of the money returns the collateral and holders keep the premium. In the money moves the locked C B T C and the strike cash in one atomic transaction. No escrow contract in between. No public mempool to front run. Collateral is locked on chain, so there is no unsecured counterparty exposure.
